subject: maths
title: Vectors

slides.heading: Vectors — direction and distance written as a single object
slides.body: A vector describes a movement that has both a size (magnitude) and a direction — unlike an ordinary number, which only has size. A column vector is written as two numbers stacked vertically in a bracket: the top number is the horizontal component (positive = right, negative = left) and the bottom number is the vertical component (positive = up, negative = down). Vectors are usually labelled with a bold letter (a) or an underlined letter (a), and the vector from point A to point B is written as AB with an arrow over it. The same column vector applied to different starting points creates parallel, equal-length movements — so two vectors are equal if and only if they have the same column vector, regardless of where they start.
slides.note: Maximum 3 sentences. Plain English. No AQA references. What is this and why does it matter.

slides.heading: Vector operations
slides.formula: Column vector: (x over y) where x = horizontal shift (+ right, − left), y = vertical shift (+ up, − down)  |  Addition: a + b = (a₁ + b₁) over (a₂ + b₂)  |  Subtraction: a − b = (a₁ − b₁) over (a₂ − b₂)  |  Scalar multiplication: k·a = (ka₁) over (ka₂)  |  Magnitude: |a| = √(x² + y²)
slides.formulaExplained: To add two column vectors, add the top numbers together and the bottom numbers together separately — never mix the rows. To subtract, subtract each component. Multiplying by a scalar k scales both components by k — this changes the magnitude but keeps the direction (or reverses it if k is negative). The magnitude (length) of vector (x, y) is found using Pythagoras: √(x² + y²). The negative of a vector reverses its direction: −a has the same length as a but points the opposite way.
slides.whenToUse: Any question involving vector paths across a diagram, proving lines are parallel, finding midpoints using vectors, or showing points are collinear. For path questions, break the journey into known vectors and combine using addition/subtraction.
slides.note: Show formula in standard notation. Explain each variable. State when this formula applies.

slides.heading: Let's work through one
slides.question: Vector a = (3 over 1) and vector b = (−1 over 4). Find: (a) a + b, (b) 2a − b.

steps.instruction: Add the vectors: add the top components and the bottom components separately.
Calculate 2a by multiplying each component of a by 2.
Subtract b from 2a: subtract each component.

slides.note: Numbers must differ from any question in the question bank for this subtopic.

slides.heading: Watch out for this

mistakes.mistake: Adding the x-component to the y-component — writing a + b = (3 + 4) or combining the rows instead of keeping them separate.
mistakes.correction: Vectors add component by component: top with top, bottom with bottom. Never add across rows. Think of the top and bottom as completely separate calculations.

mistakes.mistake: Reversing the sign when finding −a or when subtracting — forgetting that −(−1) = +1 when subtracting a negative component.
mistakes.correction: When you subtract vector b, you are adding −b. Reverse the sign of every component of b, then add. −(−1 over 4) = (1 over −4). Take care with double negatives.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing the direction of vector AB with BA — writing the vector from A to B as the negative of what it should be.
mistakes.correction: AB means 'start at A, travel to B'. BA means the reverse — exactly −AB. If AB = (4 over −2), then BA = (−4 over 2). The arrow over the letters tells you the direction.

slides.note: Minimum 2, maximum 3 mistakes. Specific not generic.

keyFacts.fact: A column vector (x over y) means move x units horizontally (+ = right) and y units vertically (+ = up). Top row is always horizontal; bottom row is always vertical.
keyFacts.examTip: Label the components before calculating: 'x-component = ..., y-component = ...' — this prevents mixing up rows in multi-step questions.

keyFacts.fact: To add vectors: add each component separately. To subtract: subtract each component. To scale: multiply each component by the scalar.
keyFacts.examTip: Never add a top component to a bottom component. Each row is an independent calculation.

keyFacts.fact: Two vectors are parallel if one is a scalar multiple of the other. Three points are collinear if the vector between any two of them is a scalar multiple of the vector between another two.
keyFacts.examTip: To prove collinearity in an exam: show one vector is a multiple of another and they share a common point — state both conditions explicitly.

note: keyFacts: 2-4 entries. Exam-precise language. These are what Mabel writes into her notes.
